Wed 11 Nov 2026 05.00 GMTLast modified on Wed 11 Nov 2026 05.06 GMTShare Prefer the Guardian on Google With his twinkling eyes and silver ponytail, M John Harrison doesn’t seem anything like his 81 years. The M stands for Michael, Mike to his friends. And last night he became the oldest author to win the Booker prize for fiction, for his 13th novel, The End of Everything. Our interview is delayed because of wifi issues, which is fitting given that the novel is about – among many things – what happens when non-human intelligence takes over.

The End of Everything is the first sci-fi novel to have won the prize in its 58-year history, which is almost as long as Harrison has been writing. “It’s interesting,” he replies, when asked if he feels vindicated, “that something that has an SF-adjacent feel can be regarded as a serious book and given the Booker prize. My problem has always been that I don’t believe in genre. I don’t believe in it in any way.” He gently wags his finger at me. It is a bit like having coffee with a cheerier, more neatly bearded Gandalf – it will surprise no one that, in his youth, Harrison read The Lord of the Rings every year for a decade.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/books/202.desc: After years on the margins, Harrison’s win for this resonantly disturbing dystopia brings the visionary writer the recognition he deserves
paras: Some have balked at a novel where none of the characters knows what’s going on, and the prose scrupulously refuses to make things any clearer for the reader. “None of this made any sense to Marnie. In that, she shared the situation of around 8 billion other human beings on the planet.” Harrison has always traded in unknowing: in Climbers, his brilliant 1989 novel about his passion for rock climbing, by the end all the main character has learned is that “I didn’t know anything about anything”.

But Harrison’s own description of The End of Everything – “What happens when all of our expectations and explanations of the world become an ongoing disaster, but we still have to make a life?” – is a strikingly topical question for 2026. It’s precisely the uncertainty, the sudden violence, the sense that something incomprehensible is happening out of the corner of one’s eye, that makes it resonate so deeply. In the postwar period, writers such as JG Ballard and Nevil Shute channelled fears of ecological breakdown and nuclear armageddon. Now, it’s Everything.

Harrison started out in science fiction – a genre famously overlooked by the Booker – publishing his first short story in Science Fantasy magazine in 1966, and becoming part of the 70s SF New Wave with Ballard and Michael Moorcock. You can find the operatic wonder and alienation of space opera in The End of Everything, though here trained on Earth: in the wake of the iGhetti, “the night was crawling with new constellations”. (A sentence that made me think of Elon Musk’s thousands of satellites.) Phillip the beachcomber – the broken man looking for revelation and a change of fortune in his shoreline discoveries – is reminiscent of the noirish space wanderers in Harrison’s back catalogue.

pg:https://www.theglobeandmail.com/world.desc: Will a party flushed with its midterm majority victory overreach?
paras: It was April 1970, three years before anyone contemplated impeaching president Richard Nixon, when representative Gerald Ford of Michigan led an unsuccessful effort to remove Justice William O. Douglas from the Supreme Court. In that decisive moment, the leader of the Republican conference in the House of Representatives issued a statement, one that would have lasting implications.

The legal basis for impeaching Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth may be debatable, and it will be debated formally and in full this week. But the truth of what, more than a half-century later, might be called the Ford Thesis, is beyond debate – and might be considered an informal codicil to the Constitution.

Whether the actions of Mr. Hegseth, the first target of the surging Democrats whose victories last week will thrust them into majority power in the House in January, meet the Article II, Section 4, Constitutional impeachment requirements will be at the centre of the searing debate that is beginning to unfold. But this “moment in history,” as Mr. Ford would put it, will examine the frontiers of the definition of “treason, bribery or other high crimes and misdemeanors” that the country’s 18th-century founders set forth.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/books/202.desc: Kazuo Ishiguro, Jeff VanderMeer, Olivia Laing and other writers weigh in on the publishing world’s genre wars
paras: Ella CreamerWed 11 Nov 2026 16.44 GMTLast modified on Wed 11 Nov 2026 18.42 GMTShare Prefer the Guardian on Google As M John Harrison was announced as the Booker prize winner on Monday evening, the 81-year-old looked gobsmacked. Decades into his career, and long overlooked by the mainstream literary establishment, he had just won a prize that has never before rewarded a writer known for science fiction, with a decidedly fantastical book.

His fans, many leading authors among them, are thrilled. “For decades it was a standard – and correct – nerd whine to point out that sentence for sentence, book for book, Harrison was one of the greatest writers out there, full stop, but that ‘mainstream’ prizes never reflected that,” says China Miéville, who last week won the Goldsmiths prize with his 1,200-page speculative novel The Rouse. Back in 2002, Miéville wrote that Harrison not having won a Booker by that point proved “the bankruptcy and back-slapping generic snobbery of the literary establishment”. Now, he says: “I am so delighted, for Harrison, and for fiction.”

While some past Booker-winning authors draw heavily on SF – Margaret Atwood, Kazuo Ishiguro, Ian McEwan – Harrison is the first winner from the “bona fide SF” sphere, said Booker prize foundation chief executive Gaby Wood on Monday. The Pulitzer and the Nobel rarely take notice of SF either, though the latter has honoured Ishiguro and Doris Lessing – both of whom are considered literary writers who dabble in SF, rather than purists, and thus perhaps considered more palatable to a wider reading public.

paras: Keza MacDonaldWed 11 Nov 2026 15.00 GMTLast modified on Wed 11 Nov 2026 17.49 GMTShare Prefer the Guardian on Google In 2015, a group of Grand Theft Auto developers from Rockstar North took their first trips to Miami to do field research for the next game in the phenomenally popular crime series. “Before you’re doing hyper-organised research trips, you’re immersing yourself in the place and its history, the vibe of it,” Rob Nelson, one of the lead developers on GTA VI, tells me. “[You see] the physical places you want to move characters through, the experiences you want them to have, and the juxtaposition between the extremes of society that are in Miami.”

This is the biggest game in the world, after all; I imagine it would be difficult to go entirely undercover. “We’re always semi-undercover,” he says. “But if you have a bunch of dorks going through a terrifying neighbourhood, you do stick out a bit.”

When Jason starts running, he hikes the six-pack of beers he’s carrying into the crook of his arm, the liquid inside the bottles sloshing around. At one point in my Vice City ridealong, Nelson gets briefly upset during a jewellery store stick-up when the placement of one of the security guards’ feet doesn’t look right. The level of detail in this game is simply out of reach for any other game developer thanks to Rockstar’s abundance of money and time, and the patience from its parent company, Take-Two Interactive.

At the center of both the strike and vote, one issue looms especially large: unaffordable housing.

Anger over the crisis boiled over in September, following the eviction of an elderly woman from the Madrid home in which she had lived since 1956. Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets in nationwide protests, prompting Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to submit a long-delayed housing bill to the Spanish parliament. When lawmakers rejected the legislation, he decided to send voters to the polls.

It is no wonder Sánchez has attempted to seize on the topic of housing in a bid to be reelected. The high price of homes is at the forefront of voters’ minds: the most recent data shows house prices are double what they were at the same time in 2015; the average Spaniard doesn’t leave their parental home until after their 30th birthday; and in some historic centers tourist accommodation accounts for 45% of the rental market.

paras: A powerful new computer simulation is allowing scientists to explore one of the most mysterious periods in cosmic history, when the universe emerged from darkness and the first stars and galaxies began to transform the cosmos.

Priced at $499.99, this effectively wipes out the $50 price hike we saw earlier this year. This discount will be applicable from 22nd November to 5th December.
From 22nd November to 29th November, you can also bag $20 off the suggested retail price of select first-party games, including Donkey Kong Bananza and Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2.
